summary: Many MPLS deployments use multipath techniques for high-bandwidth traffic, but MPLS-TP strongly discouraged them. This informational document looks at the use of multipath with MPLS and MPLS-TP and the degradation that can occur to some MPLS-TP functions.

plainLanguage.summary: Splitting traffic over several parallel roads helps carry more, but it makes it harder to tell which road a package took. This explains the tradeoffs.

questions: how does multipath work with mpls transport profile
subtitle: How to use multipath techniques with MPLS-TP for high-bandwidth networks

tldr.problem: Splitting traffic across multiple links increases bandwidth, but MPLS-TP requires all packets to follow the same path, which makes multipath difficult.
tldr.mechanism: Entropy Labels (RFC 6790) allow routers to treat MPLS-TP traffic as a fixed flow while using multipath for regular MPLS, creating a server-client layer relationship.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can deploy MPLS-TP reliably over existing multipath MPLS networks without redesigning their infrastructure.

today: RFC 7190 is an Informational RFC that remains current. It describes practical approaches that have been implemented in carrier networks. Entropy Labels are now widely supported in modern MPLS-TP implementations, making this coexistence model a viable approach for network operators.

sections.title: Introduction to MPLS and Multipath
sections.content:
Many high-bandwidth networks today split traffic across multiple parallel links to increase capacity. This is called multipath, and it comes in several forms: Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) spreads traffic across equal-cost routes; Ethernet Link Aggregation groups physical links; and Link Bundling combines them within MPLS.

However, MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) is a protocol designed for carrier-grade network operations and requires different behavior. It demands that all packets within a single logical path follow the exact same physical route and that operations, administration, and maintenance (OAM) packets follow the same path as data packets. This creates a fundamental tension: multipath splits traffic differently, which can violate MPLS-TP requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Regular MPLS networks can split packages across multiple roads to go faster. MPLS-TP networks need all packages to take the same road so they can track them. The problem is: how do you run both on the same network?

sections.title: Multipath Techniques and Their Constraints
sections.content:
Multipath techniques vary in scope. Link Aggregation creates a logical link from multiple physical Ethernet interfaces under one logical identifier. ECMP in routing protocols distributes traffic across equal-cost paths, often spreading even a single flow across different routes. Link Bundling in MPLS is similar: multiple component links are treated as a single unit, but traffic can be spread across the component links using hash-based load splitting.

The key issue is that MPLS-TP's OAM requirements include fate-sharing: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance packets must follow the same path as user data packets. Additionally, Loss Measurement OAM requires that packets not be reordered. When traffic splits across multipath links, these guarantees become impossible unless extra care is taken.
sections.plainLanguage: When traffic splits across different roads, some packages might arrive out of order or take completely different routes. MPLS-TP tools need every package to stay together so they can count them and check that nothing got lost.

sections.title: MPLS as a Server Layer for MPLS-TP
sections.content:
The document describes a solution: use regular MPLS with multipath as a server layer that carries MPLS-TP as a client layer. The key mechanism is Entropy Labels, defined in RFC 6790. An Entropy Label is an additional MPLS label inserted above the MPLS-TP label that directs multipath load-balancing. Routers hash on the Entropy Label to select a component link, then deliver all packets with the same Entropy Label to that component.

For MPLS-TP LSPs (label-switched paths), the MPLS server layer assigns a single, fixed Entropy Label value to each MPLS-TP LSP. This ensures all packets within that LSP follow the same component link. Meanwhile, regular MPLS LSPs can use per-packet entropy derived from the packet's contents, allowing true load-balancing across multipath. Alternatively, for MPLS-TP LSPs that require special handling, the ingress router can identify them and apply the Entropy Label treatment, or configure them to avoid multipath links entirely.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of splitting an MPLS-TP package across roads, we add a special label that tells the router: "This package must take road 2 every time." The router honors that label for the MPLS-TP package, while still splitting regular MPLS packages across roads for speed.

sections.title: MPLS-TP as a Server Layer for MPLS
sections.content:
The reverse scenario is also discussed: using MPLS-TP as a server layer to carry large MPLS flows. When an MPLS LSP exceeds the capacity of a single component link, multiple MPLS-TP LSPs can be used to carry it, with the MPLS LSP spread across them. This avoids the efficiency loss that would occur if MPLS-TP were the only server layer.

The main disadvantage of this approach is that MPLS-TP LSPs consume Incoming Label Map (ILM) table entries, and using multiple MPLS-TP LSPs increases the number of entries required. Additionally, MPLS-TP's strict capacity allocation reduces the flexibility of carrying smaller, variable-bandwidth MPLS LSPs efficiently, creating a bin-packing problem.
sections.plainLanguage: Using MPLS-TP roads as the server layer for MPLS packages works, but it wastes space because you have to reserve exact amounts of space on MPLS-TP roads. It's like reserving a bus seat for every package even if some packages are tiny.

sections.title: Deployment Guidance and Summary
sections.content:
For first-generation MPLS-TP deployments in multipath cores, the document recommends: routers should support administrative attributes (RFC 3209) to mark paths as multipath-safe or multipath-unsafe; core routers should support Entropy Labels and the ability to apply a fixed Entropy Label value to each MPLS-TP LSP; and edge routers should be able to identify MPLS-TP LSPs through configuration, attribute affinities, or other means.

The practical result is that MPLS-TP is fully deployable in modern multipath MPLS networks. When MPLS-TP LSPs carry MPLS as a client, or vice versa, the server layer can use multipath without degrading the client layer's requirements, provided Entropy Labels are used and administrative configuration prevents MPLS-TP LSPs from traversing multipath links that do not support Entropy Label termination.
sections.plainLanguage: To make both networks work together, routers need to understand which paths support MPLS-TP, and core routers need to apply special labels to MPLS-TP traffic. Then everything works smoothly.
